en: Sound originates from space and air; emerging from the body, it reaches the mouth.
Being differentiated across various locations [of articulation], that which attains the state of phonemes (varṇa) is called "speech" (śabda). || 1 ||
The wise rightly declare that imperishable Brahman to be the supreme purifier, dwelling within the secret cave of the heart. 2.

"This is the place of articulation, this is the organ, this is the effort, and the breath is twofold; the organ is pressed by the Vṛttikāra, and this is the sequence starting from the surface of the navel. (3)
In that regard, from the places of articulation, the organs of articulation, and the efforts, the phonemes [number] sixty-three. 4.
In this regard, it is stated: for which phonemes (varṇas) is what the place of articulation, what is the cause, and what is the effort, and for which [phonemes] are these [to be understood]? 5.

The Section on Places of Articulation. Among these, first, regarding the places of articulation: 1. The vowels *a*, *u*, *ṛ*, *ḷ*, and the visarga (*visarjanīya*) are gutturals (*kaṇṭhya*). 2. The vowels *i*, *e*, *ai*, and the consonants *k*, *kh*, *g*, *gh*, *ṅ* are gutturals. 3. According to some, the *havisarjanīya* and the *urasya* [are *jihvya*].
(3) The *jihvāmūlīya* is *jihvya*.
(4) According to some, the gutturals (*kavarga*), the letter *r*, the *anusvāra*, and the *jihvāmūlīya* are *jihvya*. (5)
Some maintain that all [consonants] have their place of articulation in the mouth.
(6) i, cu, ya, and śa are palatals.
(7) ṛ, ṭu, ru, and ṣa are retroflexes. (8)
9. For some, the place of articulation for *ra* is the root of the teeth.
10. *ḷ*, *tu*, and *la-sa* are dental. 11. *va* is labiodental.
Some [place them] in the position of the cheeks. 12. The *u*-sounds, the *upadhmānīya*, and the labials are labial. 13. The *anusvāra* and the *yama*s are nasal. 14.
Some [teachers] maintain that the anusvāra is guttural-nasal. 15. Some [teachers] maintain that the *yamas* and the jihvāmūlīya are nasal. 16.
The vowels *e* and *ai* are gutturo-palatal. 17.

The two *o* sounds (*odautau*) have the throat and lips as their place of articulation. (18) The letters *ñ, ma, ṅ, ṇ, na* have their own respective places of articulation and the nose as their place of articulation. (19) The diphthongs (*sandhyakṣara*) consist of two phonemes each. (20)
The vowel *ṛ* with the letter *repha* [is called *sarva-ṛvarṇa*]. 21.
The section on the instruments (*karaṇa*).
The instrument (*karaṇa*) is also [to be understood here]. 1.
The tongue is the instrument for the jihvya, tālavya, mūrdhanya, and dantya [sounds]. (2) How so?
(3) For the jihvya [sounds], it is by means of the root of the tongue. (4)
5. [The production] of palatals is by the middle of the tongue.
6. [The production] of cerebrals is by the tip of the tongue.
7. Or, [the production] of dentals is by the lower part of the tip of the tongue.
8. Dentals are produced by the tip of the tongue. 9. The remaining [sounds] are produced by their own respective places and organs. 10.
This is the description of the organs of articulation.
The section on internal effort: Effort is of two kinds:
(1) internal and (2) external.
First, those produced internally: 3. The *sparśa* (contact) consonants have their organs of articulation fully touched (*spṛṣṭa*). 4.
The semi-vowels (*antasthā*) have their organs of articulation slightly touched (*īṣatspṛṣṭa*). 5.
The sibilants (*ūṣman*) have slightly opened articulation. (6) The vowels (*svara*) have fully opened articulation. (7) Among those, *e* and *o* are more fully opened. (8)
From those two, the vowel *ai*. 9.
From those two also, the vowel *ā*. 10.
The closed *a*-vowel (*saṃvṛta-akāra*). 11.
Thus ends the section on internal effort (12).
Now begins the section on external effort; first, the external [effort] (1).

The first and second letters of the classes, as well as śa, ṣa, sa, visarga, the jihvāmūlīya, the upadhmānīya, and the two *yamas*, [are so designated]. (3) The first and second [letters of each class] have an open throat (*vivṛtakaṇṭha*), are produced with an emission of breath (*śvāsānupradāna*), and are voiceless (*aghoṣa*). (4) Among the [letters of the] classes and the *yamas*, the first are "slightly aspirated" (*alpaprāṇa*); all the others are "greatly aspirated" (*mahāprāṇa*). (5)

The third and fourth letters of the classes (*varga*), the semivowels (*antasthā*), the letter *ha*, the anusvāra, and the two *yama*s—these are produced with the throat constricted (*saṃvṛtakaṇṭha*), have nasal resonance as their secondary emission (*nādānupradāna*), and are voiced (*ghoṣavat*). (6) Among the classes and the *yama*s, the thirds and the semivowels are weakly aspirated (*alpaprāṇa*); all others are strongly aspirated (*mahāprāṇa*). (7)
As are the third [consonants], so are the fifth. (8) Nasality is their additional quality. (9) The consonants beginning with *ka* and ending with *ma* are the stops (*sparśa*). (10)
The semivowels (*y*, *r*, *l*, *v*) are the antaḥsthās. 11.
The sibilants (*ś*, *ṣ*, *s*, *h*) are the ūṣmans. 12.
The second [consonants of each class] share the same place of articulation as the first. 13.
By the sound *ha*, the fourth [sibilants] are produced. 14.
This is the external effort (*bāhyaprayatna*). 15.
The section on the pressure of the articulatory places (*sthānapīḍaprakaraṇa*).
In this regard, the wind that produces the *sparśa* consonants presses upon the place of articulation like a mass of iron;
(1) the wind that produces the *antastha* consonants [is like] a mass of wood; (2) the wind that produces the *ūṣman* vowels and consonants [is like] a mass of wool. (3)
In this very commentary on the *Vṛttikāra-prakaraṇa*, the *Vṛttikāras* recite: "The family of the letter *a* has eighteen divisions. Regarding this:
"Due to shortness, length, and prolation; due to the application of the three accents (*traisvarya*); and due to the distinction of nasality (*ānunāsikya*)."
It is reckoned as consisting of eighteen [sounds].
(2) Thus, the *e*-vowels and so forth. (3) There are no long forms of the *ḷ*-vowel. (4)

They declare that [the vowels] have twelve varieties. (5) When they are long, whether produced by chance, by effort, or by imitation, then they say that they also have eighteen varieties. (6) Among the diphthongs (*sandhyakṣara*), there are no short ones. (7)
These also have twelve subdivisions. (8) Among the Chandogas, the Sātyamugris and Rāṇāyanīyas recite them with short vowels. (9) They also have eighteen subdivisions. (10)
The semivowels (*antasthā*), excluding the letter *r*, are of two types: nasalized (*sānunāsika*) and non-nasalized (*niranunāsika*).
(11) There are no homogeneous (*savarṇa*) sounds for the letter *r* or for the sibilants (*ūṣman*).
(12) A consonant of a particular class (*varga*) is homogeneous with another consonant of that same class. (13)

This is the sequence of the phonemes according to their order of production. In this regard, the places of articulation, the organs of articulation, and the efforts involved are now stated as they are well-known in grammar.

In this context, that place where the phonemes (varṇa) are perceived is the "place" (sthāna). (3) That by which they are produced is the "articulatory organ" (karaṇa). (4) Effort is "exertion" (prayatna). (5)
The Section on the Navel Region:
Therein, the vital air called *prāṇa*, impelled from the region of the navel and ascending upwards, is restrained with effort within one of the locations beginning with the chest.
That air, being obstructed, strikes against its location;
from that impact with the location, sound is produced in space. That is the perception of phonemes.
That is the acquisition of the essence of the phoneme (varṇa).

1. In that regard, when the articulatory organs (dhvani) are being produced, when the places of articulation (sthāna), the articulators (karaṇa), and the efforts (prayatna) touch one another, that is "contact" (spṛṣṭatā). 2.
When they touch slightly, that is "slight contact" (īṣatspṛṣṭatā). 3.
When they touch [the point of articulation] from a distance, that is *vivṛtatā* (openness). When they touch [it] from close proximity, that is *saṃvṛtatā* (closure).
Thus is the internal effort (*antahprayatna*).

Now, when this vital air called *prāṇa*, moving upward and struck back at the head, turns back and strikes the abdominal cavity, then, as that cavity is being struck, an opening (*vivāra*) arises from its being expanded, and a closure (*saṃvāra*) arises from its being contracted. 7.
Those two are *saṃvāra* (closure) and *vivāra* (opening). 8. Therein, when the throat-cavity is closed, *nāda* (sound) is produced. 9.
When the throat-cavity is opened, *śvāsa* (breath) is produced. 10.
They call those two [the guttural and labial stops] "possessing breath and emission" (*śvāsanādāvanupradāna*).
Others, however, say: "The *anusvāra* is the emission, like the resonance of a bell.

In that regard, when the *nāda* (sound) is emitted within the resonance produced by the impact on the articulatory site (*sthāna*), then, through the conjunction of the *nāda* and the resonance, "voicing" (*ghoṣa*) arises.

When the breath is emitted, it is voiceless (aghoṣa) due to its contact with the sound of the breath. 14. That [distinction] is the state of being voiced or voiceless. 15. When the air is great, it is a "great breath" (mahāprāṇa). 16.

In a short [vowel], there is little effort and little breath. (17) This is the state of having little breath or great breath. (18) Due to having great breath, it possesses the quality of *ūṣman*. (19)

When the effort is intense and pervades all the limbs, then there is a contraction of the body and the throat-cavity. (20) Due to the rapid movement of the breath, the voice becomes subtle and harsh; this they call udātta (high-pitched).
(21) But when the effort is mild, then there is relaxation of the body and expansion of the throat-cavity.
And because the movement of the breath is slow, there is smoothness; they call that the anudātta (unraised). 22.
From the conjunction of the udātta and anudātta tones, the svarita (circumflex) arises. 23.
Thus, when this effort is accomplished, the entire effort is complete. 24.

There are eight places of articulation for the phonemes: the chest, the throat, the head, as well as the root of the tongue, the teeth, the nose, the lips, and the palate. (25) The states of being touched (*spṛṣṭatva*), slightly touched (*īṣatspṛṣṭatva*), contracted (*saṃvṛtatva*), and likewise expanded (*vivṛtatva*) are said to be the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) of the phonemes. (26) Duration (*kāla*), expansion (*vivāra*) and contraction (*saṃvāra*), breath (*śvāsa*) and resonance (*nāda*), lack of voicing (*aghoṣatā*) and voicing (*ghoṣa*), slight aspiration (*alpaprāṇatā*) and great aspiration (*mahāprāṇa*), and the three vowels (*svarāḥ*).
